tables.text: Data included in the Ecopath model
Seabirds(Phoebastria nigripes, Phoebastria immutabilis, Diomedea spp.)
In the absence of biomass estimates for the Warm Pool, used estimates of the "pursuit birds" group in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean from Olson & Watters (2003) of 600 t per million km-2.
Tuck et al. (2001), (2015), Rivalan et al. (2010)

Used the average adult natural mortality estimate used in population models for wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) (M = 0.02 yr-1) and the Amsterdam Albatross (Diomedia amsterdamensis) (M = 0.029 yr-1). In the absence of estimates of fishing mortality in the Warm Pool, a precautionary estimate of fishing mortality used assuming birds incurred a mortality in the vicinity of MSY estimated as F = 0.8M = 0.0196 yr-1. Therefore, initial P/B = 0.0245 + 0.0196 = 0.0441 yr-1.

Average daily consumption by Diotnedea chrysostoma was estimated at 750g d-1 for birds averaging 3.65kg, equating to a daily ration of 20.55% body weight (BW) day-1 and an annual ration (Q/B) of 74.99 times the population biomass yr-1.
Not permitted to be landed in Warm Pool fisheries.

Estimate derived from expanded observer data for the longline and purse seine fisheries in the WCPO for 1990-2004 (Molony, 2005). Longline annual catch estimated at 1593 birds with a 100% mortality rate. Purse seine annual catch estimated at only 20 birds per year, so this did not warrant inclusion. The Warm Pool modelled region is approximately 50% of the WCPO area assessed for bycatch, so catch estimates halved. Using a mean weight of 7 kg for the most commonly caught species (Albatross, Diomedea spp.), the 2005 estimate for each fishery divided by the water surface area of the entire Warm Pool (12,086,900 km2) was 0.000000461 km-2.
Gould et al. (1997), Harrison et al. (1983), Cherel and Klages (1998)

In the absence of dietary studies of seabirds in the Warm Pool, used diet composition (by % weight) of six species of Diomedeids in the North Pacific Ocean (Hawaii), which was dominated by epipelagic squids (20-67%), fishes (9-50%), and crustaceans (5-40%) to a lesser extent migratory mesopelagic fishes, crustaceans and fishery discards. Many of these species migrate across the entire Pacific Ocean, so these diets are likely to be representative in the Warm Pool at the functional group level.
Cetaceans(Stenella longirostris, Tursiops truncates, Delphinus delphis, Grampus griseus, Globicephala macrorhynchus)

In the absence of biomass estimates for cetaceans for the Warm Pool, initially used estimate for cetaceans in a model of the pelagic ecosystem off eastern Australia (0.013 t km-2). However, given the confidence in P/B and Q/B estimates, this biomass was far too high, producing an EE of only 0.002, which should be around 0.1-0.3 for apex predators having few predators (Christensen et al. 2009). The biomass of cetaceans would also be expected to be lower in the Warm Pool due to its oligotrophic waters. Therefore, during the balancing process biomass was iteratively reduced until EE was around 0.1.

In absence of P/B estimates for the Warm Pool, produced estimate from an age and growth study of Delphinus delphis in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean using von Bertalanffy parameters L∞ = 197.2, K = 0.687 yr-1 and the natural mortality empirical equation of Pauly (1980) using a water temperature of 29° C to produce M = 0.8385 yr-1. Since this stock is not fished and rarely caught as bycatch, so F assumed to be zero. Thus P/B = 0.8385 yr-1.

Daily ration of adult Tursiops truncatus in captivity was estimated to be 4-6% BW day-1). Used the lower value (4%) as cetaceans most likely encounter prey less frequently in the wild. Thus Q/B = 14.60 yr-1.
Not permitted to be landed in Warm Pool fisheries.

Estimate derived from expanded observer data for the longline and purse seine fisheries in the WCPO for 1990-2004. Longline annual catch estimated at 2200 animals with a post release mortality of 30%. Purse seine annual catch estimated at 3500 with a mortality rate of 10%, with 85% (or 2975 animals) being caught in PSA sets. The Warm Pool modelled region is approximately 50% of the WCPO area assessed for bycatch, so the total annual catch by fishery was: longline – 1100, PSA – 1488, PSU – 262. Using a mean weight of 100 kg for the most commonly-caught species (Common dolphin, Delphinus delphis), the 2005 estimate for each fishery divided by the water surface area of the entire Warm Pool (12,086,900 km2) was 0.0000091 km-2, 0.00001231 km-2, 0.000002172 km-2, respectively.
Dolar et al. (2003), Perrin et al. (1973), Pitman and Stinchcomb (2002),

Little quantitative dietary data is available for cetaceans in the Warm Pool, except for Stenella longirostris in the Sulu Sea, Phillipines (Dolar et al. 2003). This data was supplemented by with diet composition (by % weight or volume) of Stenella spp. in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. Most of these are present in the western Pacific Ocean, so their eastern Pacific diets are likely to be representative in the Warm Pool at the functional group level. Establishment of additional predation linkages with some functional groups (e.g. dolphinfish) was necessary based on qualitative or anecdotal evidence since very little supporting quantitative information is available due to few dietary studies on cetaceans and the low incidence of predation by these larger predators.
Turtles(Caretta caretta, Chelonia mydas, Lepidochelys olivacea, Eretmochelys imbricate)
Used 0.0033 t km-2 for turtles from tropical northern and eastern Australia. Combines estimates for Chelonia mydas (0.0015 t km-2) and Dermochelys coriacea (0.0018 t km-2).

Used von Bertalanffy parameters and the natural mortality empirical equation of Pauly (1980) for Eretmochelys imbricata from tropical Australian waters of L∞ = 100 cm CL and K = 0.048 yr-1 (Limpus 1992) at 29° C water temperature, which gave M = 0.177 yr-1. Caretta caretta from the Great Barrier Reef, Australia has an L∞ = 105 cm CL and K = 0.06 yr-1 (Wabnitz and Pauly 2008) at 29° C water temperature gave M = 0.202 yr-1. An average was used (M = 0.190 yr-1) given the presumption there should be no fishing mortality on turtles.

Estimate of 1.01% BW yr-1 was experimentally derived for Caretta caretta at 20.5° C water temperature by Njoman et al. (1982). Daily ration in warmer waters of the Warm Pool (>29° C) is likely to be considerably higher, so 2% BW yr-1 was used, thus Q/B = 7.3 yr-1.
Not permitted to be landed in Warm Pool fisheries.
Unpublished SPC scientific observer data (Valerie Allain - SPC)

The number of turtles discarded dead or with unknown status in the longline fishery was estimated based on longline observer data in the Warm Pool area for the period 2000-2010 and raised to the fleet according to the effort coverage. No estimate provided for the purse seine and pole-and-line fisheries.
Bjorndal (1997), Heithaus et al. (2008), Boyle and Limpus (2008)

Averaged diet proportions across three main species Caretta caretta, Chelonia mydas, and Eretmochelys imbricate from studies conducted in the western and northern Pacific Ocean, primarily Australia and Hawaii, but probably representative of the diets of turtles in the Warm Pool at the functional group level. Predation on turtles however, is not well documented quantitatively for adults or juveniles, but reliable qualitative studies (Heithaus et al., 2008, Boyle and Limpus, 2008) justify the establishment of trophic linkages to relevant predators in the model.

Estimate derived from the 2013 Multifan-CL (MFCL) age structured stock assessment for southwest Pacific swordfish (Davies et al. 2013) for age classes 1-2 years in Area 1 in 2005. Biomass estimate of 2760.97 t was divided by ocean surface area of Area 1 (10,339,000 km2) to produce an initial estimate of 0.000267 t km-2.

The 2013 MFCL age structured stock assessment for southwest Pacific swordfish (Davies et al. 2013) estimates natural mortality (M) of age class 1- 2 years as 0.23875 yr-1. Fishing mortality (F) for small fish in 2005 in Area 1 was 0.0388 yr-1. Therefore, M + F = Z ≈ P/B was 0.2776 yr-1. P/B was too low to derive a reliable P/Q estimate, assuming daily ration was reliable. P/B would be expected to be higher in smaller fish than larger fish, so value allowed to increase slightly.

Daily ration of swordfish in the Atlantic 0.94% to 1.6% body weight (BW) day-1 (Stillwell and Kohler 1985), so 1.3% BW day-1 (Q/B = 4.745 yr-1) was used in order to produce P/Q estimates of around 0.1 yr-1.

Used diet proportions (in % weight) from published and unpublished SPC stomach contents data in the Warm Pool and central Pacific Ocean (Allain, 2010, Dambacher et al. 2010). Diet matrix supplemented with trophic connections to less frequently encountered prey in other functional groups based on studies in the adjacent tropical Coral Sea (Young et al. 2006, 2010) and anecdotal accounts (e.g. observed predation by sharks or cetaceans).

Biomass estimate of 17922.36 t was divided by the ocean surface area of Area 1 (10,339,000 km2) to produce an estimate of 0.00173 t km-2

Fishing mortality (F) in Area 1 of the 2013 MFCL assessment for large fish in 2005 was 0.140 yr-1. Therefore, M + F = Z ≈ P/B was 0.293 yr-1.

(2003). Therefore, M + F = Z ≈ P/B was 0.4291 yr-1.

No value available for Makaira nigricans in the Warm Pool, so daily ration assumed to be similar to Kajikia audax in tropical Mexican waters, estimated to be 3.6% BW day-1 (Q/B = 13.14 yr-1) (Abitia-Cárdenas et al. 2011). However, M. nigricans grows significantly larger than K. audax and therefore is likely to have a lower daily ration. Thus, it was assumed daily ration was 2% BW day-1 (Q/B = 7.30 yr-1).

Estimate derived from the South Pacific area of the 2012 MFCL stock assessment for the southwestern Pacific Ocean (Davies et al. 2012). The 2005 biomass estimate of 5492.69 t for all age classes combined was divided by the water surface area of 42,973,000 km2 of the assessment area. The initial value used was 0.000127817 t km-2. Reduced value slightly to 6.2 x 10-5 t km-2 in order for Ecopath’s F value to match MFCL F value in 2005.

Assumed that sailfish and spearfish were as least as abundant as blue marlin and that the other species in the group were probably as abundant as striped marlin, which is reasonably low in the Warm Pool. Therefore, biomass of these groups summed to give an initial estimate of 0.000399 t km-2. Biomass decreased to 0.00022 t km-2 in order for EE to be more realistic being lower than that of sharks, which are marlin predators.
Assumed small billfish like sailfish and other Tetrapterus species have reasonably high P/B, so P/B assumed to be the same as striped marlin = 0.902 yr-1.

In the absence of species specific biomass estimates, it was assumed mako sharks would have a similar biomass as Oceanic White Tip, which was estimated using a stock assessment model. Therefore, the value of 0.000294 t km-2 was used.

Used von Bertalanffy parameters and the natural mortality empirical equation of Pauly (1980) for Isurus oxyrinchus from Baja, Mexico (Ribot-Carballal et al. 2005) of L∞  = 411 cm FL and K = 0.05 yr-1 at 29° C water temperature which gave M = 0.123. To calculate P/B of this fished stock with no available value of F, it was assumed F = 0.8M if stock is fished at or below MSY = 0.221 yr-1. Therefore, the initial P/B = 0.344 yr-1. This value was required to be increased to 0.577 yr-1 in order for P/Q to approach 0.1 for high order predators.

Estimate derived from Region 3 for all age classes of the North Pacific blue shark MFCL stock assessment (Kleiber et al. 2009). Biomass of 0.01038 t km-2 in 2002 was the most recent estimate available. However, biomass in the Warm Pool this is likely to be much lower in 2005 given the increase in catch and fishing mortality and because blue sharks prefer cooler waters.

Used von Bertalanffy parameters and the natural mortality empirical equation of Pauly (1980) for Prionace glauca from NE Brazil (Lessa 2004) of L∞ = 352.1 cm FL and K = 0.157 yr-1 at 29° C water temperature which gave M = 0.272. To calculate P/B of this fished stock with no available value of F for 2005, it was assumed F = 0.8M if stock is fished at or below MSY = 0.218 yr-1. Therefore, the initial P/B = 0.490 yr-1. This value was required to be decreased to 0.440 yr-1 in order for P/Q to approach the expected 0.1 for high order predators.

In the absence of daily ration estimates from the Warm Pool or Pacific Ocean, used daily ration estimate of 0.06% BW day-1 (Q/B = 2.19 yr-1) for Prionace glauca in the Atlantic Ocean, but increased to 3.0 given the higher water temperatures in the Warm Pool.

Therefore, M + F = Z ≈ P/B was 0.577 yr-1.

Used diet proportions (in % weight) from published and unpublished SPC stomach contents data for Carcharhinus longimanus caught in the Warm Pool and central Pacific Ocean (Allain, 2010). Little other data available for adjacent regions or other oceans, besides qualitative descriptions of prey consumed (Bonfil et al. 2008), which was integrated into the diet matrix where appropriate.

Appendix S1 – Ecopath model parameter derivation methodology
The Ecopath with Ecosim approach

We modeled the Warm Pool ecosystem using Ecopath with Ecosim software (www.ecopath.org). Ecopath trophic models describe the static state of energy flows in a food web that balances a group’s net production with all sources of mortality and migration (Polovina 1984). The software has a dynamic capability, called Ecosim, that allows forecasting of ecosystem responses to specific perturbations through time (Walters et al. 1997, Pauly et al. 2000). Ecosim re-expresses the static Ecopath model in a dynamic form, whereby the dynamics and sensitivity of the model is largely controlled by the predator consumption rates and the proportion of the prey that exist in a vulnerable state. Detailed description and discussion of Ecopath and Ecosim can be found in Walters et al. (1997), Christensen and Pauly (1992) and Christensen and Walters (2004).

The Ecopath master equation (Equation 1) balances a functional group’s net production with all sources of mortality, migration, or change for that group, such that the net production of a functional group equals the sum of (1) the total mass (or energy) removed by predators and fisheries, (2) the net biomass accumulation of the group, (3) the net migration of the group’s biomass, and (4) the mass flowing to detritus.

Bi and Bj is the standing biomass (expressed as t km-2) of prey (i) and predators (j), respectively, averaged across the modelled region. These parameters were derived using data from stock assessment models, the SEAPODYM spatial ecosystem and population dynamics model (Lehodey et al. 2008), quantitative sampling from scientific surveys, the literature, or if unknown, left to be estimated by Ecopath. The data sources and their preparation for estimating each parameter for each functional group in the model are described in Table S1. Quantitative biomass estimates of intermediate to lower trophic level groups is often a major weakness of pelagic ecosystem models (see Olson and Watters 2003), largely due to the difficulty of quantitatively sampling the standing biomass. Therefore, we used estimates of forage, and phytoplankton biomass from a 2012 version of a SEAPODYM model characterised for skipjack (Senina et al. 2008).

P/Bi is the production/biomass ratio (year-1), equivalent to natural mortality (M) for an unfished population, total mortality (Z) for a fished population (Allen 1971), or the inverse of maximum age (ω). If no information was available for natural mortality, which is common, an estimate was made using up to three empirical equations (Pauly 1980, Hoenig 1983, Jensen 1996) depending on the biological data available for a particular group.

Fishing mortality (F) data was available from stock assessments of the primary target species, but was not available for the majority of bycatch species. Therefore, conservative estimates of F were made by assuming F = 0.8(M), which can be a reasonable proxy for fishing mortality at, or below, MSY (Gabriel and Mace 1999). In these cases, initial P/B values were allowed to be decreased if required during the balancing process since they were likely to be overestimated.

EEi is the ecotrophic efficiency; the fraction of the total production of a group utilized in the system. For most forage groups (e.g. sardines) that are likely to be consumed by a large number of predators there is likely to be only a small proportion of the biomass that is not utilised by the system. Values of around 0.95 are reasonable in such cases (Christensen et al. 2009). In contrast, for large predators having few, if any, predators (e.g. large sharks), or very small, abundant and highly productive organisms (e.g. phytoplankton and zooplankton), only a small percentage of the biomass is likely to be consumed equating to EE values of around 0.1-0.3.

Q/Bj is the annual food consumption rate per unit biomass of j. This is the equivalent of annual ration, or more widely available, the daily ration (in % body weight day-1) multiplied by 365 days. This parameter was either derived from the literature (e.g. Olson and Galvan-Magana 2002, Griffiths et al. 2009a), or estimated from von Bertalanffy parameters using the empirical equation of Palomares and Pauly (1998).

DCji is the proportion of prey i in the average annual diet of predator j, represented in terms of percent wet weight. Diet data were primarily derived from stomach content analyses undertaken by the SPC Oceanic Fisheries Programme (Ecosystem Monitoring and Analysis Section) from samples collected by the observer programmes of the region. These data were supplemented, where necessary, by published and unpublished dietary data collected in studies undertaken in Australia and Papua New Guinea by the CSIRO (e.g. Griffiths et al. 2009a, Kloser et al. 2009). In the absence of dietary information for cetaceans, we used relevant data from Pauly et al. (1998b). Together, these data were used to develop the model’s initial diet matrix (Table S2), which was modified during the balancing process to produce the model’s final diet matrix (Table S3). The main difference between these two matrices is the lack of information on the predation of high trophic level species, particularly billfish and sharks, in the initial matrix. This is due to the difficulty in documenting such predation events from stomach content analysis, given the likely low frequency of these types of predation evens (e.g. sharks consuming swordfish). These predators require predation mortality to be exerted upon them in the model—as they would in the real world—to prevent their populations from unrealistically increasing perpetually. Therefore, we used expert opinion and anecdotal accounts of predation events involving these species to justify the creation of predatory links in the final diet matrix.

Yi is the total fisheries catch of a group (expressed as t km-2) averaged across the model region (i.e. Y = F*B), and includes both retained and discarded catch. These data were derived from logbook and scientific observer data held by the SPC (e.g. Williams and Terawasi 2015) (Table S4).
Ei is the net migration of i (emigration less immigration) over the course of a year, which was assumed to be zero (i.e. emigration = immigration); and

BAi is the biomass accumulation rate of i (t km-2 year-1). This is a production term that can be calculated if the biomass at the end of the year and the beginning of the following year is known. Since Ecopath is generally used as a trophic ‘snap shot’ in time, BAi is often assumed to be zero (i.e. no biomass accumulation), as it was in the current model, and biomass time series data used in Ecosim (see below) to force dynamic changes in the base Ecopath model.

The Ecopath model is a system with as many such linear equations as there are functional groups. The energy balance (conservation of matter) within each functional group is ensured with the second master equation (Equation 2):

An extension of the Ecopath model is the dynamic simulation routines of Ecosim (Walters et al. 1997, Walters et al. 2000). In Ecosim, information in the static Ecopath model is re-expressed in a dynamic form (Equation 3).

is the change in the biomass of group i (Bi) over time, gi is the efficiency of the conversion of food into growth, Qji is the rate of consumption by predators j of prey group i, Ii is the immigration rate, MOi is the non-predation natural mortality rate, Fi is the fishing mortality rate, and ei is the emigration rate.

The dynamics and sensitivity of Ecosim models is largely controlled by the consumption rates (Qji) (Equation 3), which are limited by the proportion of a given predator group’s prey that exist in a vulnerable state.  Prey vulnerability is controlled within the expression of consumption rate by a user-specified (or calculated) transfer rate of prey movement between vulnerable and invulnerable pools (vij and v’ij), thus representing the universal community stabiliser of prey refugia.  The consumption rate (Qji) expressed in Equation 4 includes the prey vulnerability parameters.

aij is the rate of effective search for prey i by predator j, Ti and Tj are the relative feeding times of prey i and predator j, Sij is the user-defined seasonal and long-term environmental forcing effects, Mij is the non-trophic mediation forcing effects, and Dj represents the effects of prey handling time by predators, which further limits consumption rates.

Parameters vij and v’ij represent prey vulnerabilities—or the rate of exchange of biomass between two prey behavioural states—a state in which all predators have full access to prey and a state in which prey have full refuge from predators.  Prey use refugia in real ecosystems and so not all prey biomass is vulnerable to predation at any given time, and predator-prey relationships are limited by behavioural and physical mechanisms. Ecosim is designed to allow the specification of the type of trophic control (Lotka-Volterra type vs. donor control) that mediates any interaction in the food web. Maximum consumption rates are hypothesised, and thus the rate of exchange of biomass (vij) that a predator normally exerts. For high prey vulnerability (vij) the functional relationship approximates a mass-action flow, or Lotka-Volterra type interaction implying a strong ‘top-down’ effect. For low prey vulnerabilities the functional relationship approaches a donor-controlled (bottom-up) flow rate so vij is the maximum possible instantaneous mortality rate that j can cause on i (Walters et al. 1997).

Prey vulnerabilities can be specified by adjusting the proportion of prey in vulnerable and invulnerable states (pools) via adjustment of the v values, which represents Lotka-Volterra (top-down) type control and pure donor control. In the real world, this mixture of trophic control is mediated by temporal or spatial refugia, or by the relative primacy of physical and biotic forces in regulating communities, i.e. predator-prey interactions. The vulnerability value for each predator-prey interaction was estimated by fitting the Ecosim model to time series of biomass, fishing mortality, and catch for functional groups where these data were available (see Appendix S3 “Calibrating the Ecosim model”).

Appendix S2 – Balancing the Ecopath model
Balancing the Ecopath model

Once all model parameters were estimated from the available datasets and literature for 2005, and multi-stanza models were constructed for swordfish, bigeye tuna, yellowfin tuna and skipjack, balancing began by first focusing on the 14 functional groups for which high quality age structured stock assessments had been undertaken.

The model was attempted to be balanced to inspect the preliminary ecotrophic efficiency (EE) and production/consumption estimates (P/Q) estimated by Ecopath for these key species. For most living groups, the primary aim during balancing is to allow Ecopath to estimate an EE of around 0.95 for species that are either heavily fished, or are expected to experience high predation rates (Christensen et al. 2009). A value of around 0.95 indicates that 95% of the biomass of the group is utilised within the system. In contrast, highly abundant and/or highly productive species (e.g. zooplankton), or high trophic level predators that have very few natural predators are expected to have low EE values of 0.1–0.3. This indicates that only a small percentage of the species’ biomass is utilised within the system, while the remainder is transferred to detritus or exported from the system.

In cases where the EE value was unrealistic—for example juvenile skipjack initially had an EE of over 1000—the biomass estimate was checked, followed by an inspection of the predation mortality and fishing mortality estimates calculated by Ecopath. Commonly, the most scientifically defensible option to reduce the EE of a group—when all other parameters appear plausible—is to slightly reduce the proportion it contributes to the diets of predators that have a very high biomass or are highly productive. The converse applies where the EE is too low, requiring greater predation mortality when all other parameter values are considered valid. These are common approaches used by Ecopath practitioners since the diet composition of most marine predators is often highly variable in space and time and an Ecopath model attempts to capture this variability for a single year. In many respects the initial diet composition of a group should be viewed as a reasonable starting point with an expectation of fine tuning using knowledge of the species and the system (see Christensen et al. 2009).

After the EE values were considered reasonable, the P/Q estimate for each group was checked to ensure it was biologically realistic. In most cases, P/Q should be between 0.1 and 0.3. In cases where P/Q was unrealistic, such as for Wahoo initially having a P/Q of 0.001, the P/B and Q/B values were inspected and revised appropriately. It was often the case that daily ration estimates from the literature were underestimated or unreliable, while the P/B value was underestimated due to poor von Bertalanffy growth parameters from which natural mortality (M) was estimated, or a lack of fishing mortality information, which was generally the case for bycatch species. Further searches of the literature or sourcing unpublished work or expert opinion often provided more reliable information that assisted in producing more reasonable P/B estimates.
Once the aforementioned process was completed for the groups having the most reliable information, and then applied sequentially to prey of these groups occupying lower trophic levels, and so on.
Diagnostics of Ecopath model validity and stability

On completion of the balancing process, we followed ‘best practice’ (Heymans et al. 2016) and “PREBAL” (Link 2010) diagnostics to test the biological and ecological validity and overall stability of the balanced model, which is summarised in Figure S1. The primary ‘rule of thumb’ proposed by Link (2010) is that biomass of functional groups in the model should span 5-7 orders of magnitude and decline at a rate of around 5-10% with increasing trophic level. Figure S1a shows the biomass of functional groups in the Warm Pool model ranging from 0.000057 t km-2 to 10.95 t km-2—slightly more than 6 orders of magnitude. Biomass decreased with increasing trophic level at a rate of 22%, with values of the majority of groups being close to the regression line.
Both P/B and Q/B values are expected to decline with increasing trophic level (Link 2010, Heymans et al. 2016), which was the case for both parameters in the Warm Pool model (Figure 1Sb and 1Sc).

Finally, the gross food conversion efficiency (P/Q) of each functional group should only produce a fraction of the biomass it has consumed (Heymans et al. 2016), usually on the order of 0.05-0.3 (Christensen et al. 2009). All functional groups had P/Q values of between 0.05-0.3 with the exception of four groups, which represent special cases. Seabirds and Sea turtles had a P/Q of 0.01 and 0.026, respectively since their production is quite low. Seabirds, such as albatross, have a very low natural mortality rates (i.e. P/B) (Tuck et al. 2001) due to high parental investment, but have high consumption rates (Q/B) to satisfy their high metabolic demands, thus resulting in a very low P/Q value. Similarly, Sea turtles are long-lived and also have a low natural mortality, but have a reasonably high Q/B due to the consumption of low energy prey, primarily gelatinous zooplankton. In contrast, “Mesopelagic fish and crustaceans” and “Migratory mesopelagic fish and crustaceans” had slightly higher than expected P/Q values (0.32-0.34) owing to their very high productivity and biomass that is required to sustain very high predation mortality from a range of open ocean predators as a ‘wasp waist’ group (Griffiths et al. 2013), as is indicated by the high EE values for these groups of 0.988 and 0.993, respectively.

Figure S1. PREBAL diagnostics showing a) biomass, b) P/B, c) Q/B, and P/Q values for each living functional group in the balanced Warm Pool Ecopath model. Asterisks denote primary producer groups for which a Q/B is not applicable.

Once we confirmed that the underlying biological and ecological assumptions of the Ecopath model had been satisfied using the recommendations of Link (2010) and Heymans et al. (2016), the thermodynamic stability of the Warm Pool model was assessed. The model was transferred to Ecosim and run for 1000 years in the absence of fishing to assess the model’s temporal stability and to observe whether any group went extinct, increase indefinitely, or demonstrate erratic or oscillatory trends in their biomass. The model produced a stable ‘flat line’ for all functional groups with no indication of temporal instability. These diagnostic tests confirmed that the Ecopath model was robust and was ready to be used for forecasting changes to the structure of the Warm Pool ecosystem under specific fishery and/or environmental scenarios specified in Ecosim.
Appendix S3 – Calibrating the Ecosim model
Fitting the Ecosim model to time series data

Once the Ecopath model was confirmed to be internally stable and ecologically realistic, we sought to optimise the reliability of predictions in Ecosim scenario modelling by calibrating the model to 111 data time series consisting of biomass, and/or fishing mortality and/or catch data for 37 of the 44 living functional groups. The data types used and their sources are detailed in Table S5. Although several data time series for economically important species extended from 1952 to 2010, data for years prior to around 1980 were considered unreliable due to various data reporting issues. Therefore, we used the years 1952–1980 for essentially ‘burning in’ the Ecosim model but focus on the years after 1980.

The data for the 37 functional groups were imported into Ecosim and weighted according to the perceived reliability of the data and its relative importance in driving the model fitting. The 30 most sensitive interactions between predators and prey were identified using the non-linear search procedure within Ecosim. The prey vulnerability rate (v, see Equation 4) for the most sensitive predator-prey interactions were then iteratively adjusted by 1% until the sums of squares error (SS) was minimised to produce the ‘best’ model fit to the time series data. This process was repeated 20 times—with v values being reset before each iteration— to minimise the chance of the nonlinear search procedure becoming ‘trapped’ in local parameter minima. The matrix of vulnerability values by predator/prey interaction that contributed to the fit with the lowest SS from the 20 iterations was saved as the ‘optimal’ vulnerability matrix, which is shown in Table S6.

In searching for the best combination of vulnerability values, the time series data were linked to an estimated trend of primary productivity anomalies, in the form of a forcing function, forced upon the “Large phytoplankton” group. A variance value of 10 was used for the model fitting, implying that the model should attempt to capture any abrupt variability in the biomass and catch data through time. This procedure did not reduce the SS and so the forcing function was removed and not included in any of the final Ecosim simulations.

Once the optimal vulnerability search was complete, vulnerability values (v) were inspected to ensure they were ecologically realistic. Although some adjustments to vulnerabilities and feeding time parameters often resulted in better visual fits of the model to observed data, they often resulted in a poorer statistical fit (lower SS) or required unrealistic parameter values, so they were disregarded. Further detailed descriptions of fitting Ecosim models to time-series data can be found in Christensen et al. (2005).

We were also interested in better understanding whether the Ecosim model was improved by including bycatch time series data, since it is common to only have reliable time series for commercially important species, which have generally been subjected to some type of stock assessment. We assessed the influence of bycatch data by removing it from the data used to calibrate the model, and recalibrated the model 10 times, as described above, and selected the best model with the lowers SS. Our results showed that the mean SS for fits where bycatch was removed was lower (SS = 52053 ± SD 1688) than for fits made using all data (SS = 55809 ± SD 1832). Although removal of bycatch data resulted in a better statistical fit, owing to fewer parameters being estimated, the quality of the model fits to observed data were substantially worse. Figure S2 shows the model fits to observed data using all data and where bycatch data were removed for four target species representing different trophic levels, and two commonly caught shark species. Clearly, the fits to observed data for most species were degraded following bycatch data removal, especially for Large bigeye tuna and Large skipjack. When the bycatch data was removed, the biomass predictions of the two shark bycatch species varied significantly in magnitude and trend.

Appendix S4 – Ecological indicators
Mixed Trophic Impact

Mixed Trophic Impact (MTI) is a sensitivity analysis within Ecopath that allows the strongest trophic interactions to be identified. This can be useful both in terms of understanding important trophic relationships, but also for identifying any possible errors or anomalies that may have occurred during model construction or the model balancing process. Results of MTI are best represented graphically—owing to the large number of combinations of predator-prey interactions—and are shown in Figure 2 in the main manuscript.
Keystone groups

The MTI analysis primarily identifies the strongest trophic interactions as a result of abundant and/or productive species preying upon species with lower biomass and productivity. However, some of the most important ecological interactions can occur when species that have relatively low biomass have an important predatory role in structuring an ecosystem. These species are often considered “keystone” species and can have a disproportionally large influence on the structure of the ecosystem relative to their biomass (Paine 1995). Results from Ecopath’s “Keystoneness” analysis for the Warm Pool model are given in Table S7, showing Ecopath’s keystone index for each functional group and its relative total impact on the ecosystem.
Table S7. Results from Ecopath’s “Keystoneness” analysis of the Warm Pool model, showing the keystone index and the relative total impact measure for each functional group.
Ecological indicators

Fulton et al. (2005) undertook a simulation study using two ecosystem models and found that indicators at the community or ecosystem level were the most reliable indicators of ecosystem change under fishing. They found no single indicator was able to provide a complete representation of the ecosystem and suggest that simultaneous use of a variety of indicators is likely to be required to detect the full range of impacts from fishing.

Fulton et al. (2005) found that useful ecosystem indicators from Ecopath are the Fishing in Balance index (FIB) and the average trophic level of the catch (TLc). In a recent Ecopath modelling study investigating the effects of fisheries and climate change on the northwest Pacific marine ecosystem, Ainsworth et al. (2011) found that Kempton’s Q index adapted for ecosystem models (see Ainsworth and Pitcher 2006) was a particularly useful indicator for assessing changes in the diversity and biomass of high trophic level species (>TL 3). Such an indicator is highly relevant to the Warm Pool ecosystem since the pelagic fisheries in the region target large predatory tunas, billfish and tuna-like species. Therefore, FIB, TLc and Kempton’s Q were three indicators of ecosystem change chosen for use in scenario modelling of the Warm Pool model. A description of each indicator is provided below.
Fishing in Balance (FIB) index

The FIB index (Pauly et al. 2000) provides an indication whether fisheries are balanced in ecological terms and not causing disruption to the functionality of the ecosystem. FIB is defined for any year i as:

where Y is the catch, TL is the mean trophic level of the catch, TE is the transfer efficiency (i.e. the ratio between the sum of export from a specified trophic level plus the flow that is transferred to the next trophic level, and the throughput of the specified trophic level), while 0 is the year used as a baseline, in this case 2005. FIB can provide an indication of overfishing when catches do not increase as expected (or a decrease in TLc) given available productivity in the system, or if the effects of fishing are sufficient to compromise the functionality of the ecosystem (FIB<0). In contrast, FIB can indicate an expansion of the fishery (e.g. increase in diversity and/or biomass of bycatch) (FIB>0).
Mean trophic level of the catch (TLc)

The mean trophic level of the catch (TLc) is an indicator whether fisheries are changing their fishing or targeting practices in response to changes in the abundance or catchability of traditional target species. Kempton’s Q index

Kempton’s Q index describes the slope of the cumulative species log-abundance curve and measures the diversity and evenness of the component of the ecosystem composed of species or functional groups with a trophic level greater than 3 (Kempton and Taylor 1976, Ainsworth and Pitcher 2006). This was considered a particularly useful indicator for assessing ecosystem changes as targets or bycatch in the Warm Pool fisheries generally occupy trophic levels higher than 3.
